content: Group A streptococcus (GAS) is responsible for 20% to 40% of pharyngitis cases in children, with the remaining cases primarily caused by viral infections. Rapid antigen detection tests (RADTs) provide a diagnosis for GAS at the point of care within five to ten minutes, offering a faster alternative to traditional throat cultures. The objective of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of RADTs in identifying GAS in children with pharyngitis. Additionally, the study aimed to compare the diagnostic performance of two major types of RADTs: enzyme immunoassays (EIA) and optical immunoassays (OIA), using both indirect and direct comparisons. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, CDSR, DARE, MEDION, and TRIP, covering studies published between January 1980 and July 2015. They also tracked related citations via PubMed, manually reviewed reference lists of included studies and relevant articles, and screened articles citing the included studies using Google Scholar. The inclusion criteria required studies to compare RADTs for GAS pharyngitis against throat culture on blood agar plates in microbiology laboratories, specifically in children seen in ambulatory care settings. Two independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts, assessed full texts for inclusion, and performed data extraction and quality assessment using the QUADAS-2 tool. A bivariate meta-analysis was used to estimate the overall sensitivity and specificity of RADTs and to explore heterogeneity across studies. The accuracy of EIA and OIA tests was compared using both indirect and direct evidence. A total of 98 unique studies were included in the review, encompassing 116 test evaluations and 101,121 participants. The overall methodological quality of the included studies was poor, with a high risk of bias in patient selection (73% of test evaluations) and the reference standard used (43% of test evaluations). Among studies where all participants underwent both RADT and throat culture (105 test evaluations; 58,244 participants; median GAS prevalence of 29.5%), RADTs demonstrated a summary sensitivity of 85.6% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 83.3% to 87.6%) and a summary specificity of 95.4% (95% CI: 94.5% to 96.2%). Sensitivity showed substantial variability across studies, while specificity was more consistent. There was no evidence of a trade-off between sensitivity and specificity. Study-level characteristics, such as the use of enrichment broth before plating, mean age and clinical severity of participants, and GAS prevalence, did not explain the observed heterogeneity in accuracy. The sensitivity of EIA and OIA tests was found to be comparable, with summary sensitivities of 85.4% and 86.2%, respectively. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the summary estimates of sensitivity and specificity were stable in studies with a low risk of bias. The authors concluded that in a population of 1000 children with a GAS prevalence of 30%, approximately 43 cases of GAS would be missed by RADTs. Whether RADTs can be used as a stand-alone test to rule out GAS depends on the specific epidemiological context. The specificity of RADTs is sufficiently high to minimize unnecessary antibiotic use. Based on these findings, it is expected that among 100 children with strep throat, 86 would be correctly identified by the rapid test, while 14 would be missed and not receive antibiotic treatment.
